items.title: 24.6.1 Acidic and Basic Properties of Amino Acids

source_refs.note: Topic 24.6.1, as printed (PDF 130); the two equilibria as equation blocks and the pH scheme redrawn.

blocks.text: Amino acids are amphoteric, i.e., they show both acidic and basic properties. However, they are less acidic than most carboxylic acids, and are less basic than most amines. In fact, the acidic part of the amino acid molecule is –NH₃⁺, group, not –COO⁻ group, and the basic part is -COO⁻ group, not –NH₂, group. RNH₃⁺ is a weaker acid than RCOOH, as shown below:
In the aqueous solution, an equilibrium exists between the dipolar ion and a cationic and an anionic form of an amino acid.

blocks.alt: H3N+-CH(R)-COOH (cationic form, predominant at low pH) in equilibrium, with OH- over and H+ under the arrows, with H3N+-CH(R)-COO- (dipolar ion, predominant at isoelectric pH), which is in equilibrium in the same way with H2N-CH(R)-COO- (anionic form, predominant at high pH).
blocks.caption: Cationic form, dipolar ion and anionic form of an amino acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 130).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed pH scheme has an extra ‘+ OH⁻’ after the dipolar ion; OH⁻ is the reagent over the arrow, not a product, so it is left out.

For each amino acid, there is specific pH at which the concentration of the zwitter ion reaches its maximum value. This pH is called the isoelectric point (pI), and each amino acid has its own unique pI.
